topic: planning and scheduling an overnight sourdough bake in a small bakery

provenance.author: subagent-en-b
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is pure batch arithmetic on the same bake, base is a diagnostic conversation about a late finish

a: Here are five doughs for tomorrow: country, rye, spelt, seeded, and a small batch of focaccia.
Their flour weights are twelve, six, four, five, and three kilograms, in that same order.
Sort the five doughs from heaviest to lightest and give me the running total after each one.
Then convert every flour weight into a water weight at seventy-eight percent hydration, rounded to the gram.
Finish with one line listing the total flour, the total water, and the combined dough weight.
base: Our overnight bake keeps drifting late, and the last two racks leave the oven after the shop opens.
We mix at four in the afternoon, and the first loaves go in around five the next morning.
The rye is always the one holding everything up, even though it is the smallest batch.
The bakery is cold at night, maybe fifteen degrees, and nothing seems to move on schedule.
Where would you start looking for the hour we keep losing somewhere in that long stretch?

a: Sorted heaviest to lightest: country twelve, rye six, seeded five, spelt four, focaccia three kilograms of flour.
Running totals after each dough are twelve, eighteen, twenty-three, twenty-seven, and thirty kilograms of flour.
Water at seventy-eight percent gives country nine thousand three hundred sixty grams and rye four thousand six hundred eighty.
Seeded takes three thousand nine hundred, spelt three thousand one hundred twenty, focaccia two thousand three hundred forty.
Totals are thirty kilograms of flour, twenty-three thousand four hundred grams of water, fifty-three thousand four hundred grams of dough.
base: The cold room is the first thing I would measure, because fifteen degrees stretches a rye bulk badly.
Rye acidifies fast but rises slowly when it is chilled, so it can look sluggish for hours.
I would want the actual dough temperature after mixing, not the room reading on the wall.
A two degree gap at mix time can easily become an hour of waiting by dawn.
Do you take any temperature at all when the doughs go into their tubs for the night?

a: Now add the levain: each dough takes twenty percent levain calculated on its own flour weight.
List the levain weight for all five doughs in the same heaviest-to-lightest order as before.
Also give me salt at two percent of flour, rounded to the nearest five grams.
Group the three wheat doughs in one block and the rye and focaccia in another.
Label each block with its bin number, one for the wheat and two for the rest.
base: We measure nothing after mixing, we just look at the tubs and guess from the domes.
The mixer runs eight minutes on second speed and the room is warmer then, near twenty degrees.
By midnight the shutters are down and the front of the bakery drops several degrees more.
The rye tub sits nearest the door, which now sounds like a poor place for it.
Would moving that tub to the shelf above the ovens be enough on its own?

a: Levain at twenty percent, heaviest first: country two thousand four hundred grams, rye one thousand two hundred.
Then seeded one thousand grams, spelt eight hundred grams, and focaccia six hundred grams of levain.
Bin one, the wheat block: country salt two hundred forty, seeded one hundred, spelt eighty grams.
Bin two takes rye salt one hundred twenty grams and focaccia salt sixty grams, at two percent.
Across all five doughs that is six thousand grams of levain and six hundred grams of salt.
base: Moving the rye above the ovens would help, though it may swing the other way in summer.
What you really want is a stable spot around twenty-two degrees rather than the warmest corner available.
I would also shorten the rye bulk and let it finish in the tin instead.
Rye rarely rewards a long bulk; it does better with a short one and a longer proof.
How firm is the rye when you scale it, and does it hold a shape at all?

a: One correction before we go further: the seeded dough is five and a half kilograms of flour.
Recalculate its water, levain, and salt only, and leave the other four doughs untouched.
Then give me the three new totals for flour, water, and levain across the whole bake.
After that, list the five doughs in the order they should enter the oven tomorrow.
Put rye first, then country, then spelt, then seeded, with the focaccia going in last.
base: The rye scales soft and it spreads on the bench within a minute of shaping.
We use eighty-five percent hydration on it, which is what the old recipe card says.
Nobody here has changed that number in years and the flour supplier switched last autumn.
The bags look the same but the loaves have been flatter since about November.
Could a different rye flour really cost us a whole hour of proofing time?

a: Seeded at five and a half kilograms takes four thousand two hundred ninety grams of water.
Its levain becomes one thousand one hundred grams and its salt one hundred ten grams.
New totals are thirty and a half kilograms of flour and twenty-three thousand seven hundred ninety grams of water.
Total levain rises to six thousand one hundred grams for the five doughs together.
Oven order as you asked: rye first, then country, then spelt, then seeded, with focaccia last.
base: A flour change can absolutely cost an hour, especially with rye and its damaged starch.
New crop or a different mill will drink water differently at the same stated hydration.
I would drop the rye to seventy-eight percent and see whether it holds a shape better.
Then keep the bulk short, thirty minutes, and give the tins a longer final proof.
Do you still have a few kilos of the old flour to run a proper comparison?

a: Last thing: convert the whole bake into bags of flour at twenty-five kilograms per bag.
Tell me how many full bags I need and what remains in the open bag.
Then split the total water into two vessels of equal volume and give me each figure.
Give me the oven schedule as five start times beginning at five in the morning.
Space the loads twenty-five minutes apart and list them with the dough name beside each time.
base: There are two sacks of the old flour left in the store room, maybe forty kilos.
We could bake both versions on the same night if the schedule allows a second mix.
The bench space is tight after midnight, though, with the country doughs already divided.
Two rye tubs side by side would mean stacking, and stacked tubs run warmer inside.
Is a stacked tub going to spoil the comparison we are trying to make here?

a: Thirty and a half kilograms of flour is one full bag plus five and a half kilograms.
Split the water evenly and each vessel holds eleven thousand eight hundred ninety-five grams.
Oven starts are rye at five, country at five twenty-five, and spelt at five fifty.
Seeded goes in at six fifteen and focaccia at six forty, twenty-five minutes apart throughout.
That is an oven window of one hour and forty minutes from the first load to the last.
base: Stacked tubs will spoil it, since the middle of a stack can sit two degrees warmer.
Put them side by side on the shelf above the ovens and swap their positions halfway.
Better still, halve both batches so each one fits a single tub on the bench.
Scale, shape, and tin them within the same ten minutes so nothing else differs.
Record dough temperature at mix, at the end of bulk, and just before the tins go in.

a: Print me a short checklist of the four steps in order for the night crew.
Step one is mixing, step two is bulk, step three is shaping, step four is proofing.
Put the clock time next to each step for the rye batch and nothing else.
Mixing begins at four in the afternoon and the tins go into the oven at five.
Use a bulk of thirty minutes and a proof filling the remaining time until then.
base: That sounds workable, and halving both batches costs us nothing but two extra tins.
I will write the temperatures on the tub lids so the night crew records them.
One worry is the seeded dough, which shares the bench and the same shaping window.
If the rye takes longer to shape, the seeded loaves will sit around waiting.
Should the seeded batch go into the cold room while the rye is being handled?

a: Rye night checklist, step one: mix at sixteen hundred, eight minutes on second speed.
Step two is bulk from sixteen ten until sixteen forty, thirty minutes as instructed.
Step three is scaling and shaping between sixteen forty and sixteen fifty-five, then tinning immediately.
Step four is the proof from sixteen fifty-five until five in the morning, roughly twelve hours.
Load the tins into the oven at five and hold that order for the rest of the night.
base: Yes, park the seeded tub in the cold room for the twenty minutes the rye needs.
Cold slows it enough that it will hold while the bench is busy with rye.
Bring it back out just before shaping so the surface does not skin over.
Write down when it went in and when it came out, on the lid again.
Two nights of that and the flour puzzle should settle itself from the notes alone.
